title: GLP-1 Weight-Loss Drugs May Cut Cancer Risk by Up to 70 Per Cent. Five ASCO Studies Explain Why South Asians Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: Pancreatic, lung, breast and blood cancers all showed significant reductions among GLP-1 users in studies covering nearly 900,000 patients presented this week
body:
Five separate studies presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting this week have landed on the same conclusion: GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs — the class that includes semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) — appear to substantially reduce the risk of developing several of the deadliest cancers.

## The Numbers Are Hard to Dismiss

The scale of the findings is striking. A Cleveland Clinic study of 12,000 type 2 diabetes patients found that those taking GLP-1 injections had up to 50 per cent lower risk of progressing to stage four cancer across lung, liver, bowel and breast cancers, compared with patients on other diabetes medications called gliptins.

A separate study from Jefferson Einstein Hospital in Philadelphia, tracking 68,000 people at high risk of lung cancer, found a 31 per cent reduction in lung cancer diagnoses among GLP-1 users. University of Pennsylvania researchers observed a roughly 30 per cent lower breast cancer rate among 217,000 women at a screening clinic who were on the drugs.

The most dramatic figure came from pancreatic cancer — one of the deadliest forms with a five-year survival rate below 13 per cent. Among 572,000 high-risk individuals, cases were 71 per cent lower in the GLP-1 group. Blood cancers showed a similar pattern: a study of 29,000 people found up to a 30 per cent reduction in leukaemia and related malignancies.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

South Asians have among the world's highest rates of type 2 diabetes. Indians develop the condition at lower BMI thresholds than most other populations, and the prevalence among Indian Americans now exceeds 20 per cent. Millions in the diaspora are already taking or considering GLP-1 medications for blood sugar control or weight management.

The cancer-protective signal, if confirmed in randomised controlled trials, would fundamentally change the calculus around these drugs. A medication many NRIs already use for metabolic health could simultaneously lower their risk of cancers that disproportionately affect South Asian populations.

## How These Drugs Might Fight Cancer

The mechanism likely runs through several channels. GLP-1 drugs reduce fat mass, which in turn lowers circulating oestrogen — a known driver of breast and uterine cancers. They also reduce chronic inflammation, a well-established promoter of tumour growth.

At a molecular level, GLP-1 receptors are expressed in several tissues beyond the pancreas, and early laboratory research suggests the drugs may directly influence cellular pathways involved in cancer development. Excess insulin, common in type 2 diabetes, is itself a growth factor for certain tumours; by improving insulin sensitivity, these drugs may remove one of cancer's fuel sources.

## The Caveats Are Real

These are observational studies, not randomised controlled trials. Patients who take GLP-1 drugs may differ from those who do not in ways that independently affect cancer risk — they may be more health-conscious, more likely to attend regular screenings, or have different comorbidity profiles.

The ASCO researchers were careful to note that the findings establish correlation, not causation. Randomised trials specifically designed to test the cancer hypothesis would take years to complete. But the consistency of the signal across five independent studies, different cancer types, and different research institutions has elevated this from a curiosity to a serious area of investigation.

## What NRIs Should Consider

If you are already taking a GLP-1 drug for diabetes or weight management, these findings suggest the medication may be doing more than you realise. If you are weighing whether to start one, the emerging cancer data adds another dimension to that conversation — though it should not be the sole reason to begin treatment.

Discuss the findings with your physician, particularly if you have a family history of the cancers mentioned. The cost of these drugs remains significant — Ozempic runs around $900 per month without insurance in the US — but for diaspora families with elevated metabolic and cancer risk, the benefit-to-cost equation may be shifting.

**Sources:** American Society of Clinical Oncology 2026 Annual Meeting presentations; Cleveland Clinic study (12,000 patients, GLP-1 vs gliptin comparison); Jefferson Einstein Hospital studies (68,000 lung cancer cohort; 572,000 pancreatic cancer cohort); University of Pennsylvania (217,000 breast screening cohort); Indiana/Florida universities (29,000 blood cancer cohort)
